abstract: Mutation rates are evolvable traits that respond to selection partly through the associations of modifier alleles with other variants affecting individual fitness. Yet, these variants can be subject to various selective regimes, whose respective role in shaping the evolution of mutation rates remains incompletely understood. To clarify the links between the fitness landscape and selection on mutation rates, we analyse a multi-locus continuum-of-alleles model where traits can affect both individual fitness and the mutation rates expressed across loci. We obtain a closed hierarchical system of moments describing the change in the distribution of traits, and thus in mutation rates, under small trait variation. We find that variation in mutation rates across individuals builds skew in the trait distribution, which plays a key role in the evolution of mutation rates; to track such asymmetries, we go beyond classical normal closure and adapt a cumulant-neglect method. We show that positive mutation rates are favoured by indirect selection out of evolutionary equilibrium (under directional, fluctuating or diversifying selection) and selected against at equilibrium (under homogenising selection). We illustrate these cases with a two-trait model, which we also study using individual-based simulations to evaluate the robustness of our deterministic results to genetic drift. Beyond these examples, our results classify the selective mechanisms acting on mutation rates and rank their importance according to the local shape of the fitness landscape and the variational properties of the population. This provides an account of the different ways selection can act on transmission fidelity in large populations.
